exam-collection-geo-500.question_text: What is the etymological meaning of the Greek root word 'Geo' in Geography?
exam-collection-geo-500.option_c: Earth
options: Water
Land
Earth
Sky
exam-collection-geo-500.explanation: The word Geography is derived from Greek words 'Geo ' meaning Earth and ' Graphein' meaning to write, describe, or map.
exam-collection-geo-500.text: What is the etymological meaning of the Greek root word 'Geo' in Geography?

exam-collection-geo-500.question_text: Who was the ancient Greek scholar who first coined the term 'Geography ' and defined it as the ' description of the Earth'?
exam-collection-geo-500.option_c: Era tos thenes of Cyrene
options: Ptolemy
Richard Hartshorne
Era tos thenes of Cyrene
Fred Schaefer
exam-collection-geo-500.explanation: Era tos thenes (c. 276–194 BC) first coined the term 'Geography' and calculated the circumference of the Earth with remarkable precision.
exam-collection-geo-500.text: Who was the ancient Greek scholar who first coined the term 'Geography ' and defined it as the ' description of the Earth'?

exam-collection-geo-500.question_text: Which branch of geography studies climate zones, atmospheric processes, and storms?
exam-collection-geo-500.option_c: Biogeography
options: Geomorphology
Climatology
Biogeography
Oceanography
exam-collection-geo-500.explanation: Climatology is the systematic study of the Earth's climate and weather patterns over long-term temporal scales.
exam-collection-geo-500.text: Which branch of geography studies climate zones, atmospheric processes, and storms?

exam-collection-geo-500.question_text: What does the contemporary scope of geography encompass?
exam-collection-geo-500.option_b: Only human cultural and political systems
exam-collection-geo-500.option_c: Both physical environmental systems and human spatial activities and their interrelationships
options: Only physical Earth surface features
Only human cultural and political systems
Both physical environmental systems and human spatial activities and their interrelationships
Neither physical nor human features
exam-collection-geo-500.explanation: Geography integrates both the physical environment and human socio-economic spatial distributions and human-environment interactions.
exam-collection-geo-500.text: What does the contemporary scope of geography encompass?

exam-collection-geo-500.question_text: Which core theme of geography involves the study of how human societies adapt to, depend on, and modify their physical environment?
exam-collection-geo-500.option_c: Human-Environment Interaction
options: Location
Place
Human-Environment Interaction
Region
exam-collection-geo-500.explanation: Human-Environment Interaction examines the reciprocal relationship: how humans modify nature (irrigation, dams) and adapt to environmental constraints (housing, agriculture).
exam-collection-geo-500.text: Which core theme of geography involves the study of how human societies adapt to, depend on, and modify their physical environment?

exam-collection-geo-500.question_text: What is the core distinction between climate 'mitigation ' and climate ' adaptation'?
exam-collection-geo-500.option_a: Mitigation aims to reduce green house gas emissions and enhance carbon sinks, while adaptation involves adjusting human and natural systems to mode rate harm from actual or expected climate impacts
exam-collection-geo-500.option_b: Mitigation is only for wealthy countries while adaptation is for developing countries
exam-collection-geo-500.option_c: Both mean identical actions
exam-collection-geo-500.option_d: Adaptation stops all future climate change
options: Mitigation aims to reduce green house gas emissions and enhance carbon sinks, while adaptation involves adjusting human and natural systems to mode rate harm from actual or expected climate impacts

Both mean identical actions
Adaptation stops all future climate change

exam-collection-geo-500.option_a: To achieve middle-income country status by 2025 while maintaining zero net green house gas emissions growth through sustainable development pillars
exam-collection-geo-500.option_c: To clear forests for industrial estates
options: To achieve middle-income country status by 2025 while maintaining zero net green house gas emissions growth through sustainable development pillars
To increase coal consumption
To clear forests for industrial estates
To abandon renewable hydroelectric development
exam-collection-geo-500.explanation: Ethiopia's CRGE strategy aims to build a carbon-neutral, climate-resilient economy based on four pillars: agriculture, fores try (afforestation/reforestation), renewable electricity, and efficient transport/industry.

exam-collection-hawas-500-eng.passage:
Last spring, employees of the Hartville Corporation organized a weeklong strike to protest poor working conditions and unreasonable company policies. The strike resulted in huge financial losses for the company and the threat of a national boycott on Hartville products. The situation resulted in the formation of an employee task force, supported by Hartville management, to review circumstances that led to the strike. The task-force findings follow:
- Hartville’s overtime pay schedule is well below the national level, and overtime is mandatory at least once a week.
- Employees working in the manufacturing department have an alarmingly high rate of repetitive stress injury. The equipment they are working with is extremely old and dangerous and does not meet current health and safety standards. The task force recommended that equipment be evaluated and brought up-to-date immediately.
- Sick and personal day policies are unclear. Employees report conflicting and/or confusing policies relating to sick and personal days, which have resulted in numerous misunderstandings about procedures and allowances as well as unfair disciplinary action.
- In the past four years, five pregnant women with clean work records were terminated soon after their pregnancies were public. In all five cases, the grounds for firing were not specifically cited, although one of the employees was told by her immediate supervisor that new mothers make very unreliable employees.
- Hartville’s upper management is largely unaware of the dissatisfaction of employees. There is evidence that middle management withholds vital information leading to upper management’s underestimation of the severity of employee discontent.

exam-collection-hawas-500-eng.passage:
Mental and physical health professionals may consider referring clients and patients to a music therapist for a number of reasons. It seems a particularly good choice for the social worker who is coordinating a client’s case. Music therapists use music to establish a relationship with the patient and to improve the patient’s health, using highly structured musical interactions. Patients and therapists may sing, play instruments, dance, compose, or simply listen to music. The course of training for music therapists is comprehensive. In addition to formal musical and therapy training, music therapists are taught to discern what kinds of interventions will be most beneficial for each individual patient.
Because each patient is different and has different goals, the music therapist must be able to understand the patient’s situation and choose the music and activities that will do the most toward helping the patient achieve his or her goals. The referring social worker can help this process by clearly communicating each client’s history. Although patients may develop their musical skills, that is not the main goal of music therapy. Any client who needs particular work on communication or on academic, emotional, and social skills, and who is not responding to traditional therapy, is an excellent candidate for music therapy.

exam-collection-hawas-500-eng.passage:
1. Critics say that current voting systems used in the United States are inefficient and often lead to the inaccurate counting of votes. Miscounts can be especially damaging if an election is closely contested. Those critics would like the traditional systems to be replaced with far more efficient and trustworthy computerized voting systems.
2. In traditional voting, one major source of inaccuracy is that people accidentally vote for the wrong candidate. Voters usually have to find the name of their candidate on a large sheet of paper containing many names—the ballot—and make a small mark next to that name. People with poor eyesight can easily mark the wrong name. The computerized voting machines have an easy-to-use touch-screen technology: to cast a vote, a voter needs only to touch the candidate’s name on the screen to record a vote for that candidate; voters can even have the computer magnify the name for easier viewing.
3. Another major problem with old voting systems is that they rely heavily on people to count the votes. Officials must often count up the votes one by one, going through every ballot and recording the vote. Since they have to deal with thousands of ballots, it is almost inevitable that they will make mistakes. If an error is detected, a long and expensive recount has to take place. In contrast, computerized systems remove the possibility of human error, since all the vote counting is done quickly and automatically by the computers.
4. Finally some people say it is too risky to implement complicated voting technology nationwide. But without giving it a thought, governments and individuals alike trust other complex computer technology every day to be perfectly accurate in banking transactions as well as in the communication of highly sensitive information.

exam-collection-hawas-500-eng.section_instruction: Read the passage about Asthma and answer the question.
exam-collection-hawas-500-eng.passage:
No longer is asthma considered a condition with isolated, acute episodes of bronchospasm. Rather, asthma is now understood to be a chronic inflammatory disorder of the airways—that is, inflammation makes the airways chronically sensitive. When these hyperresponsive airways are irritated, airflow is limited, and attacks of coughing, wheezing, chest tightness, and breathing difficulty occur.
Asthma involves complex interactions among inflammatory cells, mediators, and the cells and tissues in the airways. The interactions result in airflow limitation from acute bronchoconstriction, swelling of the airway wall, increased mucus secretion, and airway remodeling. The inflammation also causes an increase in airway responsiveness. During an asthma attack, the patient attempts to compensate by breathing at a higher lung volume in order to keep the air flowing through the constricted airways, and the greater the airway limitation, the higher the lung volume must be to keep airways open.
Although causes of the initial tendency toward inflammation in the airways of patients with asthma are not yet certain, to date the strongest identified risk factor is atopy. This inherited familial tendency to have allergic reactions includes increased sensitivity to allergens that are risk factors for developing asthma. Some of these allergens include domestic dust mites, animals with fur, cockroaches, pollens, and molds. Additionally, asthma may be triggered by viral respiratory infections, especially in children.
By avoiding these allergens and triggers, a person with asthma lowers his or her risk of irritating sensitive airways. A few avoidance techniques include: keeping the home clean and well ventilated, using an air conditioner in the summer months when pollen and mold counts are high, and getting an annual influenza vaccination. Of course, asthma sufferers should avoid tobacco smoke altogether. Smoke increases the risk of allergic sensitization in children, increases the severity of symptoms, and may be fatal in children who already have asthma. Most exacerbations can be prevented by the combination of avoiding triggers and taking anti-inflammatory medications. An exception is physical activity, which is a common trigger of exacerbations in asthma patients. However, asthma patients should not necessarily avoid all physical exertion, because some types of activity have been proven to reduce symptoms. Rather, they should work in conjunction with a doctor to design a proper training regimen, which includes the use of medication.
In order to diagnose asthma, a healthcare professional must appreciate the underlying disorder that leads to asthma symptoms and understand how to recognize the condition through information gathered from the patient’s history, physical examination, measurements of lung function, and allergic status. Because asthma symptoms vary throughout the day, the respiratory system may appear normal during physical examination.

exam-collection-bio-g9-525.question_text: Q1 (Unit 4). Suppose you want to preserve your milk by eliminating disease Causing organisms. Which of the following methods would you use?
exam-collection-bio-g9-525.option_a: Boiling the milk in water 120°C under high pressure
exam-collection-bio-g9-525.option_b: Heating the milk for 2 hours at 160°C
exam-collection-bio-g9-525.option_c: Heating the milk for 30 minutes at 63°C
exam-collection-bio-g9-525.option_d: Exposing the milk to UV-radiation
options: Boiling the milk in water 120°C under high pressure
Heating the milk for 2 hours at 160°C
Heating the milk for 30 minutes at 63°C
Exposing the milk to UV-radiation
exam-collection-bio-g9-525.explanation: Pasteurization (Holder method: 63°C for 30 minutes, or HTST: 72°C for 15 seconds) destroys pathogenic bacteria like Mycobacterium bovis without altering milk nutrients.

exam-collection-bio-g9-525.question_text: Q2 (Unit 4). In medical microbiology, how do pathogens interact with host defenses and antimicrobial controls?
exam-collection-bio-g9-525.option_a: All microorganisms are pathogenic and cannot be control led by physical sterilization
exam-collection-bio-g9-525.option_b: Pathogenic microbes cause disease by toxin production or tissue invasion, while vaccines, antiseptics, and antibiotics prevent or disrupt microbial replication
exam-collection-bio-g9-525.option_c: Viruses can reproduce on lifeless nutrient agar media
exam-collection-bio-g9-525.option_d: Antiseptics are taken internally to cure systemic infections
options: All microorganisms are pathogenic and cannot be control led by physical sterilization
Pathogenic microbes cause disease by toxin production or tissue invasion, while vaccines, antiseptics, and antibiotics prevent or disrupt microbial replication
Viruses can reproduce on lifeless nutrient agar media
Antiseptics are taken internally to cure systemic infections
exam-collection-bio-g9-525.explanation: Microbial pathology involves host-pathogen interactions. Preventive measures include vaccination and sanitation, while chemical controls include antibiotics, disinfectants, and antiseptics.

exam-collection-bio-g10-497.question_text: Q2 (Unit 2 - Heredity). Suppose a certain DNA molecule has 300 bases and 30% of them are found to be adenine. The number of cytosine would be:
exam-collection-bio-g10-497.explanation: By Chargaff's rules, Adenine = Thymine = 30% each (60% total). Cytosine + Guanine = 40% total, so Cytosine = 20%. 20% of 300 = 60 cytosine bases.

exam-collection-bio-g10-497.question_text: Q1 (Unit 3 - Homeostasis & Human Health). The eye lens is flexible in shape. This allows to:
exam-collection-bio-g10-497.option_a: Control the amount of incoming light
exam-collection-bio-g10-497.option_b: Accommodate near and distant objects
exam-collection-bio-g10-497.option_c: Transmit different colors of light
exam-collection-bio-g10-497.option_d: Pass more light in dim condition
options: Control the amount of incoming light
Accommodate near and distant objects
Transmit different colors of light
Pass more light in dim condition
exam-collection-bio-g10-497.explanation: Accommodation is the reflex adjustment of the curvature of the crystal line lens by ciliary muscles and suspensory ligaments to focus images of near or far objects precisely on the retina.

exam-collection-bio-g10-497.question_text: Q2 (Unit 3 - Homeostasis & Human Health). In human homeostasis, how do the nervous and endocrine systems regulate internal physiological conditions?
exam-collection-bio-g10-497.option_a: Internal physiological conditions fluctuate entirely with environmental changes
exam-collection-bio-g10-497.option_b: Neural reflex arcs provide rapid targeted responses while endocrine hormones mediate sustained feed back regulation of blood glucose, temperature, and osmoregulation
exam-collection-bio-g10-497.option_c: Glucagon reduces elevated blood glucose levels
exam-collection-bio-g10-497.option_d: Endocrine glands secrete hormones through ducts into the external environment
options: Internal physiological conditions fluctuate entirely with environmental changes
Neural reflex arcs provide rapid targeted responses while endocrine hormones mediate sustained feed back regulation of blood glucose, temperature, and osmoregulation
Glucagon reduces elevated blood glucose levels
Endocrine glands secrete hormones through ducts into the external environment
exam-collection-bio-g10-497.explanation: Homeostasis maintains internal physiological constancy (blood glucose, water/electrolyte balance, core temperature, arterial pH) via coordinated negative feed back loops med i ated by nervous receptors and endocrine hormone secret i ons.

exam-collection-bio-g10-497.option_b: It is polarized
exam-collection-bio-g10-497.option_c: It has an action potential
exam-collection-bio-g10-497.option_d: It is depolarized
options: Its outside membrane becomes negative
It is polarized
It has an action potential
It is depolarized
exam-collection-bio-g10-497.explanation: In a resting neuron, the membrane is polarized with a resting potential of approximately -70 mV (excess positive charge outside due to Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase).

exam-collection-bio-g10-497.option_a: Detoxification of alcohol and drugs
exam-collection-bio-g10-497.option_b: Production of bile salts
exam-collection-bio-g10-497.option_c: Conversion of glycogen into glucose
exam-collection-bio-g10-497.option_d: Deamination of excess amino acids
options: Detoxification of alcohol and drugs
Production of bile salts
Conversion of glycogen into glucose
Deamination of excess amino acids
exam-collection-bio-g10-497.explanation: Glucagon released by pancreatic alpha cells binds to hepatic receptors, stimulating glycogenolysis (breakdown of glycogen into glucose) to raise low blood glucose levels.

exam-collection-bio-g10-497.question_text: Q2 (Unit 4 - Plant Physiology). In plant physiology, what mechanisms facilitate photosynthetic synthesis, transpiration, and hormonal growth regulation?
exam-collection-bio-g10-497.option_a: Phloem conducts water uni direction ally from roots to leaves without metabolic energy
exam-collection-bio-g10-497.option_b: Chloroplasts capture radiant energy to produce carbohydrates, the transpiration stream pulls water and minerals through xylem, and auxins/cytokinins coordinate directional growth
exam-collection-bio-g10-497.option_c: Stomata remain open permanently in all environmental conditions
exam-collection-bio-g10-497.option_d: Ethylene stimulates apical dominance and inhibits all fruit ripening
options: Phloem conducts water uni direction ally from roots to leaves without metabolic energy
Chloroplasts capture radiant energy to produce carbohydrates, the transpiration stream pulls water and minerals through xylem, and auxins/cytokinins coordinate directional growth
Stomata remain open permanently in all environmental conditions
Ethylene stimulates apical dominance and inhibits all fruit ripening
exam-collection-bio-g10-497.explanation: Higher plants manufacture organic nutrients through oxygenic photosynthesis, absorb and translocate water/minerals via xylem under transpiration pull, and regulate growth and tropisms using phytohormones (auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins, ethylene, ABA).

exam-collection-bio-g10-497.option_b: Chloroplasts capture radiant energy to produce carbohydrates, the transpiration stream pulls water and minerals through xylem, and auxins/cytokinins coordinate directional growth
exam-collection-bio-g10-497.option_c: Stomata remain open permanently in all environmental conditions
exam-collection-bio-g10-497.option_d: Ethylene stimulates apical dominance and inhibits all fruit ripening
options: Phloem conducts water uni direction ally from roots to leaves without metabolic energy
Chloroplasts capture radiant energy to produce carbohydrates, the transpiration stream pulls water and minerals through xylem, and auxins/cytokinins coordinate directional growth
Stomata remain open permanently in all environmental conditions
Ethylene stimulates apical dominance and inhibits all fruit ripening
exam-collection-bio-g10-497.explanation: Higher plants manufacture organic nutrients through oxygenic photosynthesis, absorb and translocate water/minerals via xylem under transpiration pull, and regulate growth and tropisms using phytohormones (auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins, ethylene, ABA).

exam-collection-bio-g10-497.question_text: Q2 (Unit 5 - Natural Resource Conservation). In natural resource conservation, what strategies ensure sustainable ecosystem management and biodiversity preservation?
exam-collection-bio-g10-497.option_a: Uncontrol led deforestation and monoculture farming enhance ecological stability
exam-collection-bio-g10-497.option_b: Establishing national parks, protected areas, reforestation, and sustainable agro-ecological practices preserve endemic biodiversity and mitigate global warming
exam-collection-bio-g10-497.option_c: Non-renewable minerals can be rapidly regenerated through biological cycles
exam-collection-bio-g10-497.option_d: Ex situ conservation is only conducted in natural forest reserves
options: Uncontrol led deforestation and monoculture farming enhance ecological stability
Establishing national parks, protected areas, reforestation, and sustainable agro-ecological practices preserve endemic biodiversity and mitigate global warming
Non-renewable minerals can be rapidly regenerated through biological cycles
Ex situ conservation is only conducted in natural forest reserves
exam-collection-bio-g10-497.explanation: Natural resource conservation balances sustainable utilization with active habit at preservation (in situ reserves and ex situ genebanks), preventing species extinction and mitigating climate change impacts.

exam-collection-bio-g10-497.question_text: Q4 (Unit 5 - Natural Resource Conservation). Deforestation contributes to global warming. This is because it:
exam-collection-bio-g10-497.option_a: Decreases the absorption of heat by water bodies
exam-collection-bio-g10-497.option_b: Increases the rate of photosynthesis resulting the production of more oxygen
exam-collection-bio-g10-497.option_c: Decreases the amount of oxygen in the atmosphere
exam-collection-bio-g10-497.option_d: Increases the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere

Increases the rate of photosynthesis resulting the production of more oxygen
Decreases the amount of oxygen in the atmosphere
Increases the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere
exam-collection-bio-g10-497.explanation: Trees act as major carbon sinks. Clearing forests eliminates photosynthetic carbon sequestration and releases stored carbon as green house CO₂ upon burning or decaying.

exam-collection-bio-g10-497.option_b: Establishing national parks, protected areas, reforestation, and sustainable agro-ecological practices preserve endemic biodiversity and mitigate global warming
exam-collection-bio-g10-497.option_c: Non-renewable minerals can be rapidly regenerated through biological cycles
exam-collection-bio-g10-497.option_d: Ex situ conservation is only conducted in natural forest reserves

Establishing national parks, protected areas, reforestation, and sustainable agro-ecological practices preserve endemic biodiversity and mitigate global warming
Non-renewable minerals can be rapidly regenerated through biological cycles
Ex situ conservation is only conducted in natural forest reserves
exam-collection-bio-g10-497.explanation: Natural resource conservation balances sustainable utilization with active habit at preservation (in situ reserves and ex situ genebanks), preventing species extinction and mitigating climate change impacts.

exam-collection-bio-g11-g12-1403.option_a: All biomolecules lack carbon and are synthesized without dehydration reactions
exam-collection-bio-g11-g12-1403.option_b: Monomeric subunits undergo condensation/dehydration reactions to form covalent polymers, stabilized by hydrogen bonding, hydrophobic interactions, and disulfide link ages
exam-collection-bio-g11-g12-1403.option_c: Proteins are composed exclusively of fatty acids and glycerol
exam-collection-bio-g11-g12-1403.option_d: Phospholipids have completely non-polar hydrophilic heads
options: All biomolecules lack carbon and are synthesized without dehydration reactions
Monomeric subunits undergo condensation/dehydration reactions to form covalent polymers, stabilized by hydrogen bonding, hydrophobic interactions, and disulfide link ages

Phospholipids have completely non-polar hydrophilic heads
exam-collection-bio-g11-g12-1403.explanation: Macromolecules are polymers synthesized by condensation reactions: monosaccharides form polysaccharides via glycosidic bonds, amino acids form polypeptides via peptide bonds, and nucleotides form polynucleotides via phosphodiester bonds.

exam-collection-bio-g11-g12-1403.option_a: All biomolecules lack carbon and are synthesized without dehydration reactions
exam-collection-bio-g11-g12-1403.option_b: Monomeric subunits undergo condensation/dehydration reactions to form covalent polymers, stabilized by hydrogen bonding, hydrophobic interactions, and disulfide link ages
exam-collection-bio-g11-g12-1403.option_c: Proteins are composed exclusively of fatty acids and glycerol
exam-collection-bio-g11-g12-1403.option_d: Phospholipids have completely non-polar hydrophilic heads
options: All biomolecules lack carbon and are synthesized without dehydration reactions
Monomeric subunits undergo condensation/dehydration reactions to form covalent polymers, stabilized by hydrogen bonding, hydrophobic interactions, and disulfide link ages
Proteins are composed exclusively of fatty acids and glycerol
Phospholipids have completely non-polar hydrophilic heads
exam-collection-bio-g11-g12-1403.explanation: Macromolecules are polymers synthesized by condensation reactions: monosaccharides form polysaccharides via glycosidic bonds, amino acids form polypeptides via peptide bonds, and nucleotides form polynucleotides via phosphodiester bonds.

exam-collection-bio-g11-g12-1403.question_text: Q1 (Grade 11 Unit 3 - Enzymes). Which of the following external factors influence the turn over rate of enzyme by completely damaging their tertiary structure?
exam-collection-bio-g11-g12-1403.option_a: Substrate concentration
exam-collection-bio-g11-g12-1403.option_b: Competitive inhibitors
exam-collection-bio-g11-g12-1403.option_c: Temperature and pH extremes
exam-collection-bio-g11-g12-1403.option_d: Reversible inhibitors
options: Substrate concentration
Competitive inhibitors
Temperature and pH extremes
Reversible inhibitors
exam-collection-bio-g11-g12-1403.explanation: Extreme heat and pH disrupt hydrogen, ionic, and hydrophobic bonds holding the delicate tertiary conform ation, causing irreversible thermal or electrostatic denaturation.

exam-collection-bio-g11-g12-1403.option_c: Transfer ases

Hydrolases
Transfer ases
Ligases

exam-collection-bio-g11-g12-1403.question_text: Q3 (Grade 11 Unit 3 - Enzymes). In enzymology, how do catalytic proteins accelerate biochemical reactions and respond to environmental modulators?
exam-collection-bio-g11-g12-1403.option_a: Enzymes alter overall free energy change (ΔG) and are irreversibly consumed in reactions
exam-collection-bio-g11-g12-1403.option_b: Enzymes act as stereospecific biological catalysts that lower activation energy (Ea) through induced fit at the catalytic active site without altering chemical equilibrium
exam-collection-bio-g11-g12-1403.option_c: Enzyme kinetics are unaffected by pH and temperature extremes
exam-collection-bio-g11-g12-1403.option_d: Non-competitive inhibitors bind directly inside the active site
options: Enzymes alter overall free energy change (ΔG) and are irreversibly consumed in reactions
Enzymes act as stereospecific biological catalysts that lower activation energy (Ea) through induced fit at the catalytic active site without altering chemical equilibrium
Enzyme kinetics are unaffected by pH and temperature extremes
Non-competitive inhibitors bind directly inside the active site
exam-collection-bio-g11-g12-1403.explanation: Enzymes lower transition state activation energy barriers through precise chemical positioning of substrate catalytic residues, accelerating reaction velocities by factors of 10⁶ to 10¹².

exam-collection-bio-g11-g12-1403.option_b: Enzymes act as stereospecific biological catalysts that lower activation energy (Ea) through induced fit at the catalytic active site without altering chemical equilibrium
exam-collection-bio-g11-g12-1403.option_c: Enzyme kinetics are unaffected by pH and temperature extremes
exam-collection-bio-g11-g12-1403.option_d: Non-competitive inhibitors bind directly inside the active site
options: Enzymes alter overall free energy change (ΔG) and are irreversibly consumed in reactions
Enzymes act as stereospecific biological catalysts that lower activation energy (Ea) through induced fit at the catalytic active site without altering chemical equilibrium
Enzyme kinetics are unaffected by pH and temperature extremes
Non-competitive inhibitors bind directly inside the active site
exam-collection-bio-g11-g12-1403.explanation: Enzymes lower transition state activation energy barriers through precise chemical positioning of substrate catalytic residues, accelerating reaction velocities by factors of 10⁶ to 10¹².

End product inhibition

exam-collection-bio-g11-g12-1403.question_text: Q55 (Grade 11 Unit 3 - Enzymes). In enzymology, how do catalytic proteins accelerate biochemical reactions and respond to environmental modulators?
exam-collection-bio-g11-g12-1403.option_a: Enzymes alter overall free energy change (ΔG) and are irreversibly consumed in reactions
exam-collection-bio-g11-g12-1403.option_b: Enzymes act as stereospecific biological catalysts that lower activation energy (Ea) through induced fit at the catalytic active site without altering chemical equilibrium
exam-collection-bio-g11-g12-1403.option_c: Enzyme kinetics are unaffected by pH and temperature extremes
exam-collection-bio-g11-g12-1403.option_d: Non-competitive inhibitors bind directly inside the active site

exam-collection-bio-g11-g12-1403.option_b: Eukaryotic cells possess compartmentalized membrane-bound organelles (mitochondria, ER, Golgi) and 80S ribosomes, while transport occurs via passive diffusion, osmosis, or ATP-dependent active transport

exam-collection-bio-g11-g12-1403.option_b: Eukaryotic cells possess compartmentalized membrane-bound organelles (mitochondria, ER, Golgi) and 80S ribosomes, while transport occurs via passive diffusion, osmosis, or ATP-dependent active transport
exam-collection-bio-g11-g12-1403.option_c: Cell membranes are rigid imper meable barriers without protein channels
exam-collection-bio-g11-g12-1403.option_d: Plant cell walls are primarily composed of peptidoglycan

exam-collection-bio-g11-g12-1403.option_a: Viruses undergo autonomous metabolic respiration outside host cells
exam-collection-bio-g11-g12-1403.option_b: Viruses are acellular obligate intracellular entities that hijack host genetic machinery, bacteria divide by binary fission, and antiretroviral/antibacterial agents target specific replication stages
exam-collection-bio-g11-g12-1403.option_c: Retroviruses transcribe DNA into RNA using reverse transcriptase
exam-collection-bio-g11-g12-1403.option_d: Gram-positive bacteria lack cell walls entirely

Gram-positive bacteria lack cell walls entirely

exam-collection-bio-g11-g12-1403.option_b: Viruses are acellular obligate intracellular entities that hijack host genetic machinery, bacteria divide by binary fission, and antiretroviral/antibacterial agents target specific replication stages
exam-collection-bio-g11-g12-1403.option_c: Retroviruses transcribe DNA into RNA using reverse transcriptase
exam-collection-bio-g11-g12-1403.option_d: Gram-positive bacteria lack cell walls entirely
options: Viruses undergo autonomous metabolic respiration outside host cells
Viruses are acellular obligate intracellular entities that hijack host genetic machinery, bacteria divide by binary fission, and antiretroviral/antibacterial agents target specific replication stages
Retroviruses transcribe DNA into RNA using reverse transcriptase
Gram-positive bacteria lack cell walls entirely
exam-collection-bio-g11-g12-1403.explanation: Microbiology covers viral replication cycles (lytic/lysogenic, retroviral reverse transcription), bacterial morphology, gram staining distinctions, and modern antiretroviral therapeutic regimens (HAART).

exam-collection-bio-g11-g12-1403.option_a: Viruses undergo autonomous metabolic respiration outside host cells
exam-collection-bio-g11-g12-1403.option_b: Viruses are acellular obligate intracellular entities that hijack host genetic machinery, bacteria divide by binary fission, and antiretroviral/antibacterial agents target specific replication stages

exam-collection-bio-g11-g12-1403.option_d: Gram-positive bacteria lack cell walls entirely

exam-collection-bio-g11-g12-1403.option_b: Genetic diversity
exam-collection-bio-g11-g12-1403.option_c: Ecosystem diversity

options: Species diversity
Genetic diversity
Ecosystem diversity
Cultural diversity

exam-collection-bio-g11-g12-1403.option_b: Numerical mutation
exam-collection-bio-g11-g12-1403.option_c: Structural mutation
exam-collection-bio-g11-g12-1403.option_d: Chromosomal mutation
options: Gene mutation (Point mutation)
Numerical mutation
Structural mutation
Chromosomal mutation
exam-collection-bio-g11-g12-1403.explanation: Gene (point) mutations alter one or a few nucleotide base pairs within a specific gene locus, such as base substitutions, insertions, or deletions.

exam-collection-bio-g11-g12-1403.question_text: Q3 (Grade 12 Unit 3 - Genetics). In molecular genetics and gene technology, what mechanisms govern DNA replication, transcription, translation, and recombinant biotechnology?
exam-collection-bio-g11-g12-1403.option_a: Genetic code is non-universal and ambiguous
exam-collection-bio-g11-g12-1403.option_b: Semi-conservative DNA replication preserves base pairing fidelity, transcription generates mRNA, translation on ribosomes synthesizes polypeptides, and restrict i on enzymes enable recombinant DNA cloning
exam-collection-bio-g11-g12-1403.option_c: Translation occurs inside the eukaryotic nucleus
exam-collection-bio-g11-g12-1403.option_d: Sickle cell anemia results from large chromosome deletions
options: Genetic code is non-universal and ambiguous

Semi-conservative DNA replication preserves base pairing fidelity, transcription generates mRNA, translation on ribosomes synthesizes polypeptides, and restrict i on enzymes enable recombinant DNA cloning
Translation occurs inside the eukaryotic nucleus
Sickle cell anemia results from large chromosome deletions
exam-collection-bio-g11-g12-1403.explanation: Molecular genetics elucidates DNA structure (double helix, Chargaff ratios), RNA processing, the trip let codon genetic code, point/chromosomal mutations, and recombinant cloning techniques.

exam-collection-bio-g11-g12-1403.question_text: Q28 (Grade 12 Unit 3 - Genetics). If in a DNA strand of 2000 bases, 30% of the base molecules are known to be thymine, how many guanine base molecules are present in the same double-stranded DNA?
exam-collection-bio-g11-g12-1403.explanation: Thymine = 30%, so Adenine = 30% (60% total A+T). Remaining 40% is Guanine + Cytosine, meaning Guanine = 20%. 20% of 2000 = 400 guanine bases.

exam-collection-bio-g11-g12-1403.option_b: Innate behaviors (reflexes, taxes, kineses, fixed action patterns) are genetically program med, while learned behaviors (habituation, imprinting, classical/operant conditioning, insight) adapt organisms to changing environments
exam-collection-bio-g11-g12-1403.option_c: Imprinting occurs continuously throughout an animal's entire adult lifespan
exam-collection-bio-g11-g12-1403.option_d: Habituation increases an animal's response to harmless recurring stimuli
options: All animal behaviors are strictly learned through operant conditioning

Innate behaviors (reflexes, taxes, kineses, fixed action patterns) are genetically program med, while learned behaviors (habituation, imprinting, classical/operant conditioning, insight) adapt organisms to changing environments

Habituation increases an animal's response to harmless recurring stimuli
exam-collection-bio-g11-g12-1403.explanation: Ethology categorizes animal behaviors into innate (genetically fixed, stereotyped) and learned (experiential modification) mechanisms that optimize for aging, predator avoidance, and social communication.

exam-entrance-1789748454208.question_text:
Which one of the following CORRECTLY shows the relative charges of an electron, proton and
neutron, respectively?
exam-entrance-1789748454208.explanation:
The fundamental subatomic particles carry specific relative electrical charges:
- **Electron ($e^-$):** carries a relative charge of $-1$.
- **Proton ($p^+$):** carries a relative charge of $+1$.
- **Neutron ($n^0$):** carries no charge, i.e., a relative charge of $0$. Thus, the relative charges of an electron, proton, and neutron, respectively, are $-1, +1, 0$.

- **Why Option C is correct:** It correctly pairs electron ($-1$), proton ($+1$), and neutron ($0$) in the requested sequence.
- **Why Option A is in correct:** It assigns $0$ to the electron and $-1$ to the neutron.
- **Why Option B is in correct:** It assigns $0$ to the electron, $-1$ to the proton, and $+1$ to the neutron.
- **Why Option D is in correct:** It assigns $0$ to the proton and $+1$ to the neutron.

exam-entrance-1789748454208.question_text: Which statement below CORRECTLY describes the Bohr's model of an atom?
exam-entrance-1789748454208.option_a: Protons and electrons are found in the nucleus.
exam-entrance-1789748454208.option_b: Electrons and neutrons are found in the nucleus.
exam-entrance-1789748454208.option_c: Protons move in circular or bits around the nucleus.
exam-entrance-1789748454208.option_d: Electrons move in circular or bits around the nucleus.
exam-entrance-1789748454208.explanation:
According to Niels Bohr's atomic model:
1. Electrons revolve around the dense, positively charged atomic nucleus in discrete, fixed circular or bits (energy levels).
2. Protons and neutrons are localized inside the central nucleus.

- **Why Option D is correct:** It accurately describes the motion of electrons in circular or bits surrounding the nucleus.
- **Why Option A is in correct:** Electrons are located in or bits outside the nucleus, not inside it.
- **Why Option B is in correct:** Electrons are outside the nucleus, while neutrons are inside.
- **Why Option C is in correct:** Protons reside within the nucleus and do not orbit around it.

exam-entrance-1789748454208.option_a: a regular repetition of chemical and physical proper ties in the Periodic Table.
exam-entrance-1789748454208.option_b: a row in the Periodic Table which contains elements with same number of shells.
exam-entrance-1789748454208.option_c:
a measure of electronegativity which runs from least electronegative to most electronegative
elements.
exam-entrance-1789748454208.option_d: a column of the Periodic Table which contains elements with similar chemical proper ties.
exam-entrance-1789748454208.explanation:
In chemistry, **period i city** refers to the recurring trends or regular repetition of physical and chemical proper ties of elements when arranged in order of increasing atomic number in the Periodic Table.

- **Why Option A is correct:** It precisely captures the concept of regular, periodic repetition of elemental proper ties.
- **Why Option B is in correct:** This defines a horizontal **period**, not period i city itself.
- **Why Option C is in correct:** Electronegativity is an example of a periodic property, but it does not define period i city.
- **Why Option D is in correct:** This defines a vertical **group** or family of elements.

exam-entrance-1789748454208.question_text: Which statement below CORRECTLY expresses hydrogen bonding? It is formed by bonding
exam-entrance-1789748454208.option_a: a hydrogen atom to an element such as sodium.
exam-entrance-1789748454208.option_b: a hydrogen atom to an element such as oxygen.
exam-entrance-1789748454208.option_c: two hydrogen atoms with equal sharing of electrons.
exam-entrance-1789748454208.option_d: two hydrogen atoms with unequal sharing of electrons.
exam-entrance-1789748454208.explanation:
A **hydrogen bond** is a strong dipole-dipole intermolecular attraction that occurs when a hydrogen atom is covalently bonded to a highly electronegative atom with a small atomic radius, specifically **Fluorine ($F$), Oxygen ($O$), or Nitrogen ($N$)**.

- **Why Option B is correct:** Oxygen is one of the highly electronegative elements capable of forming hydrogen bonds with hydrogen (e.g., in $H_2O$).
- **Why Option A is in correct:** Sodium ($Na$) is an electropositive alkali metal; bonding hydrogen to sodium forms an ionic hydride ($NaH$), not a hydrogen bond.
- **Why Options C and D are in correct:** Two hydrogen atoms bonded to each other form a nonpolar covalent hydrogen molecule ($H_2$), not a hydrogen bond.

two hydrogen atoms with unequal sharing of electrons.

exam-entrance-1789748454208.question_text: What is the bond formed between two or more atoms by sharing of electrons?
exam-entrance-1789748454208.explanation:
A **covalent bond** is formed when two or more nonmetal atoms share one or more pairs of valence electrons to achieve stable electron configurations.

- **Why Option C is correct:** Sharing of electron pairs is the defining characteristic of covalent bonding.
- **Why Option A is in correct:** An ionic bond involves the complete **transfer** of electrons from a metal to a nonmetal atom.
- **Why Option B is in correct:** A metallic bond consists of metallic cat i ons attracted to a delocalized 'sea' of valence electrons.
- **Why Option D is in correct:** Valence bond theory is a theoretical approach explaining covalent bonding, not a type of bond.
exam-entrance-1789748454208.section_instruction: Answer question 5 based on Unit 2: Chemical Bonding and Structure standards.
exam-entrance-1789748454208.text: What is the bond formed between two or more atoms by sharing of electrons?

exam-entrance-1789748454208.explanation:
**Dipole-dipole forces** are attractive electrostatic forces between the permanent positive pole of one polar molecule and the permanent negative pole of another polar molecule.

- **Why Option B is correct:** Dipole-dipole forces occur specifically between permanent polar molecules.
- **Why Option A is in correct:** Nonpolar molecules do not possess permanent dipoles and therefore do not exhibit dipole-dipole forces.
- **Why Option C is in correct:** Nonpolar molecules interact through London dispers i on forces.
- **Why Option D is in correct:** Interaction between a polar and a nonpolar molecule forms a dipole-induced dipole force.

exam-entrance-1789748454208.question_text:
Comparing the forces between molecules of similar molar masses, which one of the following
produces the weakest force?
exam-entrance-1789748454208.explanation:
When evaluating interactions among chemical species of similar molar mass:
1. **Intramolecular forces** (Covalent and Ionic bonds) are strong chemical bonds holding atoms together within compounds.
2. **Intermolecular forces** (Hydrogen bonding, Dipole-dipole, Van der Waals/London dispers i on forces) hold separate molecules together and are considerably weaker.
3. Among intermolecular forces, **Van der Waals (London dispers i on) forces** are the weakest.

- **Why Option D is correct:** Van der Waals forces are the weakest forces listed.
- **Why Options A and C are in correct:** Covalent and ionic bonds are strong intramolecular chemical forces.
- **Why Option B is in correct:** Hydrogen bonding is the strongest type of intermolecular force.

Van der-Waal's forces.

exam-entrance-1789748454208.question_text: What is a limiting reactant? It is the reactant that
exam-entrance-1789748454208.option_b: remains unreacted as the reaction proceeds.
exam-entrance-1789748454208.option_c: present in excess when the reaction goes to completion.
exam-entrance-1789748454208.option_d: completely consumed when the reaction goes to completion.
exam-entrance-1789748454208.explanation:
The **limiting reactant** (or limiting reagent) is the reactant that is completely consumed first in a chemical reaction. Once it is exhausted, the reaction stops, there by limiting the maximum amount of product that can be formed.

- **Why Option D is correct:** It correctly describes the limiting reactant as the one completely consumed at reaction completion.
- **Why Option A is in correct:** A catalyst is regenerated at the end of a reaction, not a limiting reactant.
- **Why Options B and C are in correct:** These describe the **excess reactant**, which remains part i ally unreacted after completion.

exam-entrance-1789748454208.question_text: Which statement below CORRECTLY distinguishes redox and non-redox reactions?
exam-entrance-1789748454208.option_a: Electrons are transfer red in redox reactions but not in non-redox reactions.
exam-entrance-1789748454208.option_b: Reduction occurs in redox reactions and oxidation takes place in non-redox reactions.
exam-entrance-1789748454208.option_c: Oxidation number remains the same in both redox and non-redox reactions.
exam-entrance-1789748454208.option_d: Acid-base reactions can be considered as both redox and non-redox reactions.
exam-entrance-1789748454208.explanation:
The key criterion distinguishing redox from non-redox reactions is electron transfer:
- **Redox reactions:** Involve the net transfer of electrons between species, causing changes in oxidation numbers.
- **Non-redox reactions:** Involve no transfer of electrons (e.g., acid-base neutralization or precipitation), so oxidation numbers remain constant.

- **Why Option A is correct:** Electron transfer takes place in redox reactions but not in non-redox reactions.
- **Why Option B is in correct:** Reduction and oxidation always occur concurrently within a redox reaction; non-redox reactions involve neither.
- **Why Option C is in correct:** Oxidation numbers change in redox reactions.
- **Why Option D is in correct:** Standard acid-base reactions involve proton ($H^+$) transfer, not electron transfer, so they are non-redox reactions.
exam-entrance-1789748454208.section_instruction: Answer question 9 based on Unit 2: Acid-Base Equilibria standards.
exam-entrance-1789748454208.text: Which statement below CORRECTLY distinguishes redox and non-redox reactions?
options: Electrons are transfer red in redox reactions but not in non-redox reactions.
Reduction occurs in redox reactions and oxidation takes place in non-redox reactions.
Oxidation number remains the same in both redox and non-redox reactions.
Acid-base reactions can be considered as both redox and non-redox reactions.

exam-entrance-1789748454208.question_text:
Given the reaction C (s) + CO2 (g) ⇌ 2CO (g) What is the equilibrium constant expression for
the reaction?
exam-entrance-1789748454208.explanation:
For the heterogeneous equilibrium reaction:
$$C (s) + CO_2 (g) \rightleftharpoons 2CO (g)$$

The equilibrium constant expression $K_{eq}$ is defined as the ratio of product concentrations to reactant concentrations, each raised to the power equal to its stoichiometric coefficient.

**Key rules:**
1. Pure solids ($s$) and pure liquids ($l$) have constant activity and are **omitted** from the equilibrium expression.
2. Product $CO (g)$ has coefficient $2$, giving term $ [CO] ^2$.
3. Reactant $CO_2 (g)$ has coefficient $1$, giving term $[CO_2]$.
4. Solid carbon $C (s)$ is excluded. Thus, $K_{eq} = \frac{ [CO] ^2}{[CO_2]}$.

- **Why Option B is correct:** It excludes pure solid carbon and correctly places gaseous products over reactants raised to their respective stoichiometric coefficients.
- **Why Options A and C are in correct:** They erroneously include solid carbon $ [C] $ in the expression.
- **Why Option D is in correct:** It inverted the expression (reactants over products) and included solid carbon.

exam-entrance-1789748454208.question_text:
What is the oxidation number of manganese in KMnO₄? Atomic Number K=19, Mn= 25 and
O=16
exam-entrance-1789748454208.explanation:
**Oxidation State Calculation for Potassium Permanganate ($KMnO_4$):**

1. **Fundamental Oxidation State Rules (Ethiopian Grade 11 Chemistry Unit 5):**
 - Group 1 alkali metals (Potassium, $K$) always exhibit an oxidation number of $+1$ in compounds: $ON (K) = +1$.
 - Oxygen ($O$) typically has an oxidation number of $-2$ in non-peroxide compounds: $ON (O) = -2$.
 - The algebraic sum of oxidation states in a neutral compound must equal zero ($0$).

2. **Mathematical Formulation:**
 $$\text{Sum} = ON (K) + ON (Mn) + 4 \times ON (O) = 0$$
 $$(+1) + ON (Mn) + 4(-2) = 0$$
 $$1 + ON (Mn) - 8 = 0$$
 $$ON (Mn) - 7 = 0 \implies ON (Mn) = +7$$

3. **Evaluation of Choices:**
 - **Choice A (+5):** In correct; would leave an overall net charge of $-2$.
 - **Choice B (+6):** In correct; this corresponds to manganate ion ($MnO_4^{2-}$).
 - **Choice C (+7):** **CORRECT.** Manganese in permanganate achieves its maximum $+7$ oxidation state by sharing all valence $4s^2 3d^5$ electrons.
 - **Choice D (+8):** In correct; exceeds the valence capacity of Manganese ($Z=25$).

exam-entrance-1789748454208.question_text: Silver has two known i so topes, 107Ag and 108Ag with their percent abundance of 52
exam-entrance-1789748454208.explanation:
**Calculation of Relative Atomic Mass from I so topic Abundances:**

1. **Underlying Formula (Ethiopian Grade 11 Chemistry Unit 1):**
 The relative atomic mass ($A_r$) of an element is the weighted average of the atomic masses of its naturally occur ring i so topes:
 $$A_r = \sum (\text{Mass of Isotope}_i \times \text{Fractional Abundance}_i)$$

2. **Given Parameters:**
 - Isotope 1: $^{107}\text{Ag}$ with mass $\approx 107\text{ u}$ and abundance $= 52\% = 0.52$.
 - Isotope 2: $^{108}\text{Ag}$ with mass $\approx 108\text{ u}$ and abundance $= (100 - 52)\% = 48\% = 0.48$.

3. **Step-by-Step Calculation:**
 $$A_r(\text{Ag}) = (107 \times 0.52) + (108 \times 0.48)$$
 $$(107 \times 0.52) = 55.64$$
 $$(108 \times 0.48) = 51.84$$
 $$A_r(\text{Ag}) = 55.64 + 51.84 = 107.48\text{ u}$$

4. **Evaluation of Choices:**
 - **Choice A, B, D:** In correct arithmetic values.
 - **Choice C (107.48):** **CORRECT.** Exactly matches the weighted average i so topic calculation.

exam-entrance-1789748454208.explanation:
**Definition and Class if i cat i on of Acids (Ethiopian Grade 12 Chemistry Unit 2 - Acid-Base Equilibria):**

1. **Theoretical Class if i cat i on:**
 - **Strong Acid:** An acid that under goes **complete ($100\%$) ionization** in dilute aqueous solution (e.g., $HCl, HNO_3, H_2SO_4$), resulting in a dynamic equilibrium shifted entirely to the right ($K_a \gg 1$).
 - **Weak Acid:** An acid that ionizes only **partially/to a slight extent** in aqueous solution, establishing an equilibrium where un-ionized molecules predominate ($K_a \ll 1$, such as $CH_3COOH, HF, HCN$).
 - **Concentrated vs. Dilute:** Refer to the mass/molar ratio of solute to solvent (concentration), NOT the degree of ionization.

2. **Evaluation of Options:**
 - **Choice A (Dilute acid):** In correct; describes low concentration, not ionization extent.
 - **Choice B (Strong acid):** In correct; strong acids dissociate completely.
 - **Choice C (Weak acid):** **CORRECT.** By definition, a weak acid dissociates only slightly in water.
 - **Choice D (Concentrated acid):** In correct; describes high solute-to-solvent ratio.

exam-entrance-1789748454208.question_text:
Solutions can be class if ied based upon their pH values. What is a solution whose pH value
13?
exam-entrance-1789748454208.explanation:
**Class if i cat i on of Aqueous Solutions by pH (Ethiopian Grade 12 Chemistry Unit 2):**

1. **The pH Scale and Autoprotolysis of Water at $25^\circ\text{C}$:**
 - Neutral Solution: $\text{pH} = 7.00$ where $[H_3O^+] = [OH^-] = 1.0 \times 10^{-7}\text{ M}$.
 - Acidic Solution: $\text{pH} < 7.00$ where $[H_3O^+] > [OH^-]$.
 - Basic (Alkaline) Solution: $\text{pH} > 7.00$ where $[OH^-] > [H_3O^+]$.

2. **Given Condition:**
 - For a solution with $\text{pH} = 13$:
 $$[H_3O^+] = 10^{-\text{pH}} = 10^{-13}\text{ M}$$
 $$[OH^-] = \frac{K_w}{[H_3O^+]} = \frac{10^{-14}}{10^{-13}} = 10^{-1}\text{ M} = 0.1\text{ M}$$
 Since $[OH^-] \gg [H_3O^+]$, this indicates a strongly alkaline (basic) medium (such as $0.1\text{ M } NaOH$).

3. **Evaluation of Choices:**
 - **Choice A (Amphoteric):** In correct; refers to substances acting as both acid and base.
 - **Choice B (Acidic):** In correct; acidic solutions have $\text{pH} < 7$.
 - **Choice C (Neutral):** In correct; neutral solutions have $\text{pH} = 7$.
 - **Choice D (Basic solution):** **CORRECT.** $\text{pH} = 13 > 7$ denotes a strongly basic solution.

exam-entrance-1789748454208.question_text:
Which one of the following statement CORRECTLY defines rate of reaction? The rate of a
reaction is
exam-entrance-1789748454208.option_a: the changes in concentration of reactants or products per unit time.
exam-entrance-1789748454208.option_b: the measure of the amount of energy change in a chemical reaction.

exam-entrance-1789748454208.explanation:
**Definition and Units of Reaction Rate (Ethiopian Grade 11 Chemistry Unit 4 - Chemical Kinetics):**

1. **Fundamental Rate Law Formulation:**
 The **rate of a chemical reaction** measures how rapidly reactants are consumed or products are formed over time:
 $$\text{Rate} = -\frac{1}{a}\frac{\Delta [A] }{\Delta t} = +\frac{1}{b}\frac{\Delta [B] }{\Delta t}$$
 - Units: $\text{mol}\cdot\text{L}^{-1}\cdot\text{s}^{-1}$ ($	ext{M}/\text{s}$).

2. **Analysis of Choices:**
 - **Choice A:** **CORRECT.** Standard definition: the change in molar concentration of reactants or products per unit time.
 - **Choice B:** In correct; describes enthalpy/thermochemistry ($\Delta H$).
 - **Choice C:** In correct; describes reaction mechanism/kinetics study rather than the quantitative rate.
 - **Choice D:** In correct; describes Graham's Law of Gaseous Diffusion.

exam-entrance-1789748454208.question_text:
Consider the following gaseous reversible reaction is at a state of equilibrium: PCI₃(g) + Cl₂(g)
⇌ PCI₅(g) Which of the following changes in concentration will cause the equilibrium shift to the right?
exam-entrance-1789748454208.option_a: Decreasing the concentrations of the reactants and products equivalently.
exam-entrance-1789748454208.option_b: Increasing the concentration of the reactants and products equivalently.
exam-entrance-1789748454208.option_c:
Increasing the concentrations of the reactants and decreasing the concentration of the
product.
exam-entrance-1789748454208.option_d:
Decreasing the concentrations of the reactants and increasing the concentration of the
product.
exam-entrance-1789748454208.explanation:
**Le Chatelier's Principle on Gaseous Equilibrium (Ethiopian Grade 12 Chemistry Unit 1):**

1. **Reaction System:**
 $$PCl_3 (g) + Cl_2 (g) \rightleftharpoons PCl_5 (g)$$
 The forward reaction consumes reactants ($PCl_3, Cl_2$) and produces product ($PCl_5$).

2. **Le Chatelier's Principle:**
 If a dynamic equilibrium is disturbed by changing the concentration of a constituent species:
 - **Increasing reactant concentrations ($[PCl_3]$ or $[Cl_2]$):** The system counter acts the change by consuming reactants, driving the net reaction **to the right (forward)** to produce more $PCl_5$.
 - **Decreasing product concentration ($[PCl_5]$):** The system counter acts the loss by decomposing more reactants, driving the net reaction **to the right (forward)**.

3. **Analysis of Choices:**
 - **Choice A & B:** Changing both reactants and products equivalently keeps the reaction quotient $Q_c \approx K_c$.
 - **Choice C:** **CORRECT.** Increasing $[PCl_3]$ and $[Cl_2]$ while continuously removing $[PCl_5]$ makes $Q_c < K_c$, shifting equilibrium strongly to the right.
 - **Choice D:** Decreasing reactants and adding product makes $Q_c > K_c$, driving the shift to the left.

exam-entrance-1789748454208.question_text:
Consider the following equilibrium reaction at 298 K: 2NO2 (g) ⇌ 2NO (g) + O2 (g) PnO2 = 0.75 atm PnO = 2.5 x 10⁻⁵ P02= 3.5 x 10⁻⁵ atm
What is the equilibrium constant (Kp) at this temperature?
exam-entrance-1789748454208.explanation:
**Calculation of Gaseous Equilibrium Constant ($K_p$) at $298\text{ K}$ (Ethiopian Grade 12 Chemistry Unit 1):**

1. **Equilibrium Reaction & Expression:**
 $$2NO_2 (g) \rightleftharpoons 2NO (g) + O_2 (g)$$
 The partial pressure equilibrium constant $K_p$ is expressed as:
 $$K_p = \frac{(P_{NO})^2 \cdot (P_{O_2})}{(P_{NO_2})^2}$$

2. **Given Partial Pressures:**
 - $P_{NO_2} = 0.75\text{ atm}$
 - $P_{NO} = 2.5 \times 10^{-5}\text{ atm}$
 - $P_{O_2} = 3.5 \times 10^{-5}\text{ atm}$

3. **Mathematical Step-by-Step Evaluation:**
 $$(P_{NO})^2 = (2.5 \times 10^{-5})^2 = 6.25 \times 10^{-10}\text{ atm}^2$$
 $$\text{Numerator} = (6.25 \times 10^{-10}) \times (3.5 \times 10^{-5}) = 2.1875 \times 10^{-14}\text{ atm}^3$$
 $$\text{Denominator} = (P_{NO_2})^2 = (0.75)^2 = 0.5625\text{ atm}^2$$
 $$K_p = \frac{2.1875 \times 10^{-14}}{0.5625} \approx 3.8889 \times 10^{-14} \approx 3.9 \times 10^{-14}$$

4. **Evaluation of Options:**
 - **Choice A, B, C:** In correct arithmetic values.
 - **Choice D ($3.9 \times 10^{-14}$):** **CORRECT.** Exactly matches the evaluated equilibrium constant expression.

The molecule of BrF₅ has both bonding and lone pair of electrons. Based upon these
electrons, which one the CORRECT molecular geometry of the molecule of BrF₅?
exam-entrance-1789748454208.explanation:
**VSEPR Theory and Molecular Geometry of Bromine Pentafluoride ($BrF_5$) (Ethiopian Grade 11 Chemistry Unit 2):**

1. **Valence Electron Count & Lewis Structure:**
 - Central atom Bromine ($Br$, Group 17) has $7$ valence electrons.
 - Five Fluorine atoms form $5$ single covalent $\sigma$-bonds, using $5$ electrons.
 - Remaining valence electrons on $Br$: $7 - 5 = 2$ electrons, which form **$1$ lone pair**.

2. **Steric Number & Geometrical Arrangement:**
 - Steric Number ($SN$) = $5\text{ bonding pairs} + 1\text{ lone pair} = 6$.
 - **Electron Domain Geometry:** Octahedral ($AX_5E$).
 - **Molecular Geometry (Shape):** **Square Pyramidal**.
 - The four equatorial Fluorine atoms form a square base, one axial Fluorine occupies the apex, and the lone pair occupies the opposite axial position, slightly compressing the bond angles ($< 90^\circ$).

3. **Evaluation of Options:**
 - **Choice A (Square planar):** Molecular geometry of $AX_4E_2$ (e.g., $XeF_4$).
 - **Choice B (Square pyramidal):** **CORRECT.** True shape of $AX_5E$ ($BrF_5, IF_5, ClF_5$).
 - **Choice C (Trigonal pyramidal):** Shape of $AX_3E$ (e.g., $NH_3$).
 - **Choice D (Trigonal bipyramidal):** Shape of $AX_5$ (e.g., $PCl_5$).

exam-entrance-1789748454208.question_text:
Which of the following statements CORRECTLY describes the relationship among
wave length, frequency and speed in an electromagnetic radiation?
exam-entrance-1789748454208.option_a: As the wave length increases, the frequency increases.
exam-entrance-1789748454208.option_b: As the wave length decreases, the frequency increases.
exam-entrance-1789748454208.option_c: As the wave length decreases, the speed of light increases.
exam-entrance-1789748454208.option_d: As the frequency increases, the speed of light decreases.
exam-entrance-1789748454208.explanation:
**Electromagnetic Radiation Wave Proper ties (Ethiopian Grade 11 Chemistry Unit 1):**

1. **Fundamental Wave Equation:**
 All electromagnetic waves travel through vacuum at the constant speed of light ($c \approx 3.0 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}$):
 $$c = \lambda \cdot \nu$$
 Where:
 - $c$ = Speed of light in vacuum (a universal constant).
 - $\lambda$ = Wave length (distance between wave crests in meters).
 - $\nu$ ($f$) = Frequency (oscillations per second in $\text{Hz}$ or $\text{s}^{-1}$).

2. **Inverse Relationship:**
 $$\nu = \frac{c}{\lambda}$$
 Since $c$ is constant, frequency ($
u$) is **inversely proportional** to wave length ($lambda$).
 - When wave length decreases (shorter waves like X-rays/gamma rays), frequency **increases** (higher photon energy, $E = h\nu$).
 - The speed of light in vacuum never changes with frequency.

3. **Evaluation of Options:**
 - **Choice A:** False; frequency and wave length are inversely, not directly, proportional.
 - **Choice B:** **CORRECT.** As wave length decreases, frequency increases inversely.
 - **Choice C & D:** False; speed of light in vacuum is constant ($c$).

exam-entrance-1789748454208.question_text: Which of the following organic compounds has the highest boiling point?
exam-entrance-1789748454208.explanation:
**Comparative Intermolecular Forces and Boiling Points (Ethiopian Grade 11 Chemistry Unit 6):**

1. **Types of Intermolecular Forces:**
 - **Ethanol ($CH_3CH_2OH$):** Contains a highly polarized $-OH$ hydroxyl group capable of forming strong **intermolecular hydrogen bonds** ($O-H\cdots O$) in add it i on to dipole-dipole and London dispers i on forces. Boiling point: $\approx 78.37^\circ\text{C}$.
 - **Ethanal (Acetaldehyde, $CH_3CHO$):** Polar carbonyl group with dipole-dipole interactions, but lacks hydrogen bonding between molecules. Boiling point: $\approx 20.2^\circ\text{C}$.
 - **Ethane ($C_2H_6$):** Nonpolar alkane; held only by weak London dispers i on forces. Boiling point: $-88.6^\circ\text{C}$.
 - **Ethene ($C_2H_4$):** Nonpolar alkene; held only by weak dispers i on forces. Boiling point: $-103.7^\circ\text{C}$.

2. **Conclusion:**
 Hydrogen bonding requires significantly higher thermal energy to overcome, resulting in Ethanol having the highest boiling point.

3. **Evaluation of Options:**
 - **Choice A (Ethanol):** **CORRECT.** Intermolecular hydrogen bonding gives it the highest boiling point ($78^\circ\text{C}$).
 - **Choice B, C, D:** Lack hydrogen bonding and have significantly lower boiling points.

exam-entrance-1789748454208.question_text: What is a Lewis base? It is
exam-entrance-1789748454208.explanation:
**Lewis Acid-Base Theory (Ethiopian Grade 12 Chemistry Unit 2):**

1. **Comparison of Acid-Base Definitions:**
 - **Arrhenius Theory:** Acid produces $H^+$ in water; Base produces $OH^-$.
 - **Brønsted-Lowry Theory:** Acid is a proton ($H^+$) donor; Base is a proton ($H^+$) accept or.
 - **Lewis Theory (G. N. Lewis, 1923):**
 - **Lewis Acid:** An electron-pair **accept or** (electrophile, e.g., $BF_3, AlCl_3, H^+, Fe^{3+}$).
 - **Lewis Base:** An electron-pair **donor** (nucleophile with lone pairs, e.g., $: NH_3, H_2\ddot{O}:, : Cl^-$).

2. **Analysis of Choices:**
 - **Choice A:** Brønsted-Lowry Acid (proton donor).
 - **Choice B:** Brønsted-Lowry Base (proton accept or).
 - **Choice C:** Lewis Acid (electron pair accept or).
 - **Choice D:** **CORRECT.** A Lewis base is an electron-pair donor.

exam-entrance-1789748454208.question_text:
Given the following information:
CH₃COOH (aq) ⇌ CH₃COO⁻ (aq) + H⁺ (aq) Initial concentration (mol/L) 0.2 0 0
Change -x +x +x
Equilibrium concentration 0.2 - x x x
Which of the following expression represent for the percent ionization of CH₃COOH?
exam-entrance-1789748454208.explanation:
**Percent Ionization of a Weak Acid (Ethiopian Grade 12 Chemistry Unit 2):**

1. **Definition of Percent Ionization:**
 The **percent ionization** of an acid measures the fraction of original un-ionized acid molecules that dissociate into ions at equilibrium:
 $$\text{Percent Ionization} = \left( \frac{\text{Equilibrium Concentration of } H^+}{\text{Initial Concentration of Weak Acid}} \right) \times 100\%$$

2. **Given ICE Table Parameters for Acetic Acid ($CH_3COOH$):**
 - Initial concentration $[CH_3COOH]_0 = 0.2\text{ mol/L}$.
 - Equilibrium concentration of dissociated hydronium/hydrogen ions $[H^+]_{eq} = x\text{ mol/L}$.
 - Equilibrium concentration of un-ionized acid $[CH_3COOH]_{eq} = 0.2 - x\text{ mol/L}$.

3. **Substituting into Formula:**
 $$\text{Percent Ionization} = \left( \frac{x}{0.2} \right) \times 100\%$$

4. **Evaluation of Choices:**
 - **Choice A:** In correctly uses equilibrium concentration in denominator.
 - **Choice B:** **CORRECT.** $\left(\frac{x}{0.2}\right) \cdot 100\%$.
 - **Choice C:** Represents percentage of un-ionized acid remaining.
 - **Choice D:** Inverted ratio.

exam-entrance-1789748454208.question_text: Which of the following reaction shows the action of H₂SO₄ as oxidizing agent?
exam-entrance-1789748454208.explanation:
**Action of Sulfuric Acid ($H_2SO_4$) as an Oxidizing Agent (Ethiopian Grade 12 Chemistry Unit 4 & 5):**

1. **Chemical Behavior of Concentrated $H_2SO_4$:**
 Concentrated sulfuric acid is a powerful **oxidizing agent** at elevated temperatures, where the central Sulfur atom in $+6$ oxidation state is reduced to $+4$ (in $SO_2$):
 $$Cu (s) + 2H_2SO_4 (aq) \right arrow CuSO_4 (aq) + SO_2 (g) + 2H_2O (l)$$

2. **Oxidation State Analysis:**
 - Metallic Copper: $ON (Cu) = 0 \right arrow +2$ (in $CuSO_4$); Copper is **oxidized** by losing 2 electrons.
 - Sulfur in $H_2SO_4$: $ON (S) = +6 \right arrow +4$ (in $SO_2$); Sulfur is **reduced** by gaining 2 electrons.
 - Because $H_2SO_4$ causes the oxidation of $Cu$ while itself under going reduction, it functions strictly as an **oxidizing agent**.

3. **Evaluation of Other Options:**
 - **Choice A:** Combination synthesis of acid (non-redox).
 - **Choice B:** Classic acid-base neutralization (non-redox).
 - **Choice C:** **CORRECT.** A true redox reaction demonstrating sulfuric acid's oxidizing power.
 - **Choice D:** Acid displacement reaction of nitride (non-redox).

**Class if i cat i on and Composition of Commercial Glass (Ethiopian Grade 12 Chemistry Unit 6):**

1. **Soda-Lime Glass (Window and Bottle Glass):**
 - **Raw Materials:** Silica sand ($\approx 70\%\text{ } SiO_2$), Sodium carbonate / Soda ash ($\approx 15\%\text{ } Na_2CO_3$), and Limestone ($\approx 10\%\text{ } CaCO_3$).
 - Heating these reagents at $\approx 1400^\circ\text{C}$ forms a molten mixture of sodium and calcium silicates:
 $$Na_2CO_3 + SiO_2 \right arrow Na_2SiO_3 + CO_2 (g)$$
 $$CaCO_3 + SiO_2 \right arrow CaSiO_3 + CO_2 (g)$$
 - Soda-lime glass accounts for over **$90\%$ of all manufactured glass** globally.

2. **Analysis of Other Glass Types:**
 - **Quartz glass:** Pure fused silica ($SiO_2$).
 - **Borosilicate / Pyrex glass:** Contains boron oxide ($B_2O_3$), giving high thermal shock resistance.
 - **Soda-lime:** **CORRECT.** Standard soda-lime composition.

exam-entrance-1789748454208.question_text: Which of the following catalyst is used in the Ostwald process for the production of HNO3?
exam-entrance-1789748454208.explanation:
**Industrial Synthesis of Nitric Acid via the Ostwald Process (Ethiopian Grade 12 Chemistry Unit 5):**

1. **Step-by-Step Chemistry of the Ostwald Process:**
 - **Stage 1 (Catalytic Oxidation of Ammonia):**
 Ammonia gas is mixed with excess oxygen and passed over a **Platinum ($Pt$) or Platinum-Rhodium ($Pt-Rh$) gauze catalyst** at $\approx 850-900^\circ\text{C}$:
 $$4NH_3 (g) + 5O_2 (g) \xrightarrow{Pt/Rh, 900^\circ\text{C}} 4NO (g) + 6H_2O (g) \quad (\Delta H < 0)$$
 - **Stage 2 (Oxidation of Nitric Oxide):**
 $$2NO (g) + O_2 (g) \right arrow 2NO_2 (g)$$
 - **Stage 3 (Absorption in Water):**
 $$3NO_2 (g) + H_2O (l) \right arrow 2HNO_3 (aq) + NO (g)$$

2. **Evaluation of Options:**
 - **Choice A (Pt):** **CORRECT.** Platinum (or $Pt-Rh$ wire mesh) is the catalytic agent for Ostwald oxidation.
 - **Choice B ($V_2O_5$):** Catalyst for the *Contact Process* ($2SO_2 + O_2 \right arrow 2SO_3$).
 - **Choice C ($Fe$):** Catalyst for the *Haber-Bosch Process* ($N_2 + 3H_2 \right arrow 2NH_3$).
 - **Choice D ($CuO$):** Used in organic dehydrogenation.

A student was given a standard Zn (s)/Zn^2+(aq) half-cell and another half-cell containing
copper immersed in 1.00 M CuSO4 (aq). When the Zn was connected as the anode at 25°C, the
cell potential reading on the voltmeter shows 1.1 V. Which of the following is NOT correct
regarding the cell potential measurement?
exam-entrance-1789748454208.option_a: The mass of copper was increased during the cell potential measurement
exam-entrance-1789748454208.option_b: The circuit is completed inside the cell by migration of ions through the salt bridge.
exam-entrance-1789748454208.option_c: The zinc electrode was dissolved and the blue color CuSO4 solution would fade.
exam-entrance-1789748454208.option_d: Electrons travel through the external circuit from copper cathode to the zinc anode.
exam-entrance-1789748454208.explanation:
**Galvanic (Voltaic) Daniell Cell Operation: $Zn (s) | Zn^{2+}(aq) || Cu^{2+}(aq) | Cu (s)$ (Ethiopian Grade 12 Chemistry Unit 4):**

1. **Half-Cell Reactions & Potentials at $25^\circ\text{C}$:**
 - **Anode (Negative Electrode - Oxidation):**
 $$Zn (s) \right arrow Zn^{2+}(aq) + 2e^- \quad (E^\circ_{ox} = +0.76\text{ V})$$
 Zinc dissolves into the solution, losing mass.
 - **Cathode (Positive Electrode - Reduction):**
 $$Cu^{2+}(aq) + 2e^- \right arrow Cu (s) \quad (E^\circ_{red} = +0.34\text{ V})$$
 Copper ions from $CuSO_4$ are plated onto the copper strip, increasing its mass and fading the blue color of $Cu^{2+}$.
 - **Cell Potential:** $E^\circ_{cell} = 0.76 + 0.34 = 1.10\text{ V}$.

2. **Electron and Ion Transport:**
 - In the **external wire**, electrons flow spontaneously from the **anode (Zinc)** to the **cathode (Copper)**.
 - In the **internal salt bridge**, an i ons migrate toward the anode and cat i ons migrate toward the cathode.

3. **Evaluation of Options:**
 - **Statements A, B, C:** Factually correct observations.
 - **Statement D:** **FALSE (and therefore the CORRECT answer).** Electrons travel from Zinc anode to Copper cathode, NOT from Copper to Zinc.

exam-entrance-1789748454208.explanation:
**Electrolysis of Molten Sodium Chloride (Downs Cell) (Ethiopian Grade 12 Chemistry Unit 4):**

1. **Electrolytic Dissociation of Molten Salt:**
 In the molten state, $NaCl (l)$ dissociates completely into free-moving mobile ions: $Na^+$ cat i ons and $Cl^-$ an i ons.

2. **Electrode Half-Reactions:**
 - **At the Cathode (Reduction - Negative Pole):**
 $$Na^+(l) + e^- \right arrow Na (l)$$
 - **At the Anode (Oxidation - Positive Pole):**
 $$2Cl^-(l) \right arrow Cl_2 (g) + 2e^- \quad \implies \quad Cl^-(l) \right arrow \frac{1}{2}Cl_2 (g) + e^-$$

3. **Overall Net Cell Reaction:**
 Adding both half-reactions:
 $$Na^+(l) + Cl^-(l) \xrightarrow{\text{Electrical Energy}} Na (l) + \frac{1}{2}Cl_2 (g)$$
 Or in doubled stoichiometric form: $2NaCl (l) \right arrow 2Na (l) + Cl_2 (g)$.

4. **Evaluation of Choices:**
 - **Choice A:** Represents spontaneous reverse formation.
 - **Choice B:** **CORRECT.** The exact overall electrolytic reaction.
 - **Choice C & D:** Electrolysis of water.

Na+(l) + Cl-(l) -> Na (l) + 1/2 Cl2 (g): This is the correct reaction.
H2 (g) + 1/2 O2 (g) -> H2O (g): Electrolysis of water.
H2O (g) -> H2 (g) + 1/2 O2 (g): Electrolysis of water.

exam-entrance-1789748454208.explanation:
**Electrolysis of Dilute Sulfuric Acid ($H_2SO_4$) Using Inert Platinum Elect rodes (Ethiopian Grade 12 Chemistry Unit 4):**

1. **Species in Aqueous Solution:**
 Dilute $H_2SO_4 (aq)$ contains $H_3O^+$ (or $H^+$), $SO_4^{2-}$, and solvent $H_2O$ molecules.

2. **Electrode Processes:**
 - **At Cathode (Negative Electrode - Reduction):**
 $H^+$ ions have a much higher reduction potential ($E^\circ = 0.00\text{ V}$) and are preferentially discharged:
 $$2H^+(aq) + 2e^- \right arrow H_2 (g)$$
 Hydrogen gas bubbles vigorously off the negative electrode.
 - **At Anode (Positive Electrode - Oxidation):**
 Sulfate ($SO_4^{2-}$) is extremely stable against oxidation; water ($H_2O$) is preferentially discharged:
 $$2H_2O (l) \right arrow O_2 (g) + 4H^+(aq) + 4e^-$$

3. **Evaluation of Options:**
 - **Choice A:** False; sulfate is not discharged.
 - **Choice B:** False; overall net reaction is water splitting ($2H_2O \right arrow 2H_2 + O_2$).
 - **Choice C:** **CORRECT.** $H^+$ ions are discharged at the negative cathode.
 - **Choice D:** False; loss of water increases the acid concentration over time.

occasionally
rarely

options: cancel
launch
destroy
ignore

exam-entrance-2016-eng.section_instruction: Section One: Vocabulary (Completion)
exam-entrance-2016-eng.option_a: cancel
exam-entrance-2016-eng.text: The company decided to ________ the new product next month after completing all safety tests.

exam-entrance-2016-eng.question_text: Her pers is tent hard work and dedication finally ________ in her passing the national examination with top marks.
options: resulted
failed
prevented
stopped
exam-entrance-2016-eng.explanation: 'Resulted in' is the correct phrasal verb meaning to cause or lead to a specific outcome.
exam-entrance-2016-eng.section_instruction: Section One: Vocabulary (Completion)
exam-entrance-2016-eng.option_a: resulted
exam-entrance-2016-eng.text: Her pers is tent hard work and dedication finally ________ in her passing the national examination with top marks.

exam-entrance-2016-eng.question_text: We tolerate no ________ of any kind on our premise. Everybody is treated as a human being.
options: entertainment
discrimination
nepotism
condemn ation
exam-entrance-2016-eng.explanation: The second sentence ('Everybody is treated as a human being') indicates equality and fair treatment. 'Discrimination' fits the contextually negative blank.
exam-entrance-2016-eng.section_instruction: Section One: Vocabulary (Completion)
exam-entrance-2016-eng.option_a: entertainment
exam-entrance-2016-eng.text: We tolerate no ________ of any kind on our premise. Everybody is treated as a human being.

options: scattered
concentrated
located
disarrayed
exam-entrance-2016-eng.explanation: 'Scattered' means spread far apart over a wide area, explaining why the speaker has friends in many different places across the country.
exam-entrance-2016-eng.section_instruction: Section One: Vocabulary (Completion)
exam-entrance-2016-eng.option_a: scattered
exam-entrance-2016-eng.text: My friends are ________ all over the country and I don't have any problem wherever I go. I have no worries of where to stay or what to eat.

exam-entrance-2016-eng.question_text: The noise made by a group of revolting students ________ our discussion and we had to call the police.
options: endangered
blocked
disrupted
stifled
exam-entrance-2016-eng.explanation: 'Disrupted' means interrupted or disturbed an activity or process, which describes what external noise does to an on going discussion.
exam-entrance-2016-eng.section_instruction: Section One: Vocabulary (Completion)
exam-entrance-2016-eng.option_a: endangered
exam-entrance-2016-eng.text: The noise made by a group of revolting students ________ our discussion and we had to call the police.

exam-entrance-2016-eng.question_text: Unless viable solutions are sought for our development problems, the people will keep suffering under poverty. So, let us get together and find the way out.
options: productive
sustainable
sensible
promotable
exam-entrance-2016-eng.explanation: 'Viable' in the context of solving long-term develop mental issues means capable of working successfully or enduring over time, which aligns closely with 'sustainable'.
exam-entrance-2016-eng.section_instruction: Section One: Vocabulary (Substitution)
exam-entrance-2016-eng.option_a: productive
exam-entrance-2016-eng.text: Unless viable solutions are sought for our development problems, the people will keep suffering under poverty. So, let us get together and find the way out.

exam-entrance-2016-eng.question_text: AIDS patients used to be alien ated for having HIV in their blood. Today, however, things have changed and they are treated like any healthy person.
options: stigmatized
involved
preserved
disappointed

exam-entrance-2016-eng.section_instruction: Section One: Vocabulary (Substitution)
exam-entrance-2016-eng.option_a: stigmatized
exam-entrance-2016-eng.text: AIDS patients used to be alien ated for having HIV in their blood. Today, however, things have changed and they are treated like any healthy person.

exam-entrance-2016-eng.question_text: The troop opened an attack on the enemy in a bid to capture the garrison. I know it is not going to take long.

designed
launched
dropped

exam-entrance-2016-eng.section_instruction: Section One: Vocabulary (Substitution)
exam-entrance-2016-eng.option_a: realized
exam-entrance-2016-eng.text: The troop opened an attack on the enemy in a bid to capture the garrison. I know it is not going to take long.

dismay

synergy

exam-entrance-2016-eng.section_instruction: Section One: Vocabulary (Substitution)
exam-entrance-2016-eng.option_a: power
exam-entrance-2016-eng.text: It appears the combined effort exerted by the team significantly contributed to their success. In fact, we need to take a lesson and reshape our strategy.

propagating
working
manipulating

Extended

exam-entrance-2016-eng.option_a: Eliminate
